summary: Describes changes to the sockets API, the de facto standard programming interface for TCP/IP applications, that are needed to support IPv6. The goal is to keep the portability applications enjoyed with IPv4. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo describes changes to the sockets programming interface so applications can use IPv6 addresses. It aims to keep existing IPv4 programs working and gives programs common tools for address lookup, conversion, and multicast.

questions: what is the ipv6 sockets api
subtitle: The basic socket structures and functions applications need to use IPv6 alongside IPv4.

tldr.problem: The sockets API exposes IP address sizes, and IPv6 addresses are larger than IPv4 addresses, so applications need new address structures and functions.
tldr.mechanism: The memo adds IPv6 socket address structures, interface and multicast controls, and protocol-independent name lookup and address conversion functions.
tldr.outcome: The design preserves compatibility with IPv4 applications and allows IPv6 sockets to communicate with IPv4 nodes. The memo is informational; it identifies the cited POSIX specification as the official API standard.

today: RFC 3493 is an Informational document published in February 2003. It obsoletes RFC 2553; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 3493. The text identifies the cited POSIX standard as the official sockets API specification.

sections.title: Why the Sockets API Needed Extensions
sections.content:
The socket interface is a widely used programming interface for TCP/IP applications. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits; IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, so the address-carrying parts of the interface need to support a larger value. Applications also need access to IPv6 features such as multicast.

This memo defines basic extensions for a broad range of applications. A companion document covers more specialized features, including raw sockets and IPv6 extension headers. The memo is informational and says the official sockets API specification is the cited POSIX standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs pass network addresses through the sockets interface. IPv6 addresses need more room than IPv4 addresses, so the interface needs new structures and functions while keeping old programs usable.

sections.title: Design Goals and Compatibility
sections.content:
The changes aim to preserve source and binary compatibility: existing programs should continue to work, whether run as existing binaries or recompiled. Changes should be limited, and applications should be able to communicate with IPv4 and IPv6 hosts without needing to know which address family the peer uses. IPv6 addresses in data structures should be 64-bit aligned.

The core socket functions already pass addresses through generic pointers and lengths, so their call syntax does not need to change. The memo instead adds IPv6-specific address structures, new lookup and conversion functions, and controls for features such as hop limits and multicast.
sections.plainLanguage: The API adds IPv6 support while keeping the existing socket calls and IPv4 structures available. This lets applications move to IPv6 without replacing the whole interface.

sections.title: IPv6 Address Structures and IPv4 Interoperation
sections.content:
The new address family is AF_INET6. The in6_addr structure holds one 128-bit address as sixteen 8-bit elements. The sockaddr_in6 structure carries the address family, port, flow information, IPv6 address, and scope identifier. A variant with a leading length field is described for 4.4BSD-based systems.

Applications use AF_INET6 when creating IPv6 sockets and pass IPv6 addresses in sockaddr_in6. Systems must continue supporting AF_INET and sockaddr_in, and an application may use IPv4 and IPv6 sockets at the same time. An IPv4-mapped IPv6 address stores an IPv4 address in its low-order 32 bits and uses the fixed high-order 96-bit prefix shown as ::FFFF:; it lets an IPv6 socket communicate with an IPv4 node.

The memo also defines wildcard and loopback address forms and sockaddr_storage, a structure designed to hold supported address structures with suitable size and alignment. The sin6_flowinfo field's use is not fully specified; applications should set it to zero and ignore it when returned by the system.
sections.plainLanguage: A new address structure has room for a full IPv6 address and related information. IPv4 can still be used directly, or represented inside a special IPv6 address when an IPv6 socket needs to reach an IPv4 node.

sections.title: Interface Identification and IPv6 Socket Options
sections.content:
Interface indexes are positive integers used to identify local interfaces, including when joining a multicast group. The API provides functions to map interface names to indexes, indexes to names, list all names and indexes, and free the list's allocated memory.

The new socket options use the IPPROTO_IPV6 level. IPV6_UNICAST_HOPS controls the hop limit for outgoing unicast packets. Multicast options select the outgoing interface, set the multicast hop limit, control local loopback, and join or leave a group. A process must join a group to receive its multicast datagrams; a UDP application must also bind the relevant port.

IPV6_V6ONLY restricts an AF_INET6 socket to IPv6 communication when enabled. The default is off. The memo gives running separate IPv4 and IPv6 versions of a server on the same port as one possible use.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications can select an interface, control how far multicast travels, and join or leave multicast groups. They can also choose whether an IPv6 socket accepts IPv4 communication.

sections.title: Name Lookup and Address Conversion
sections.content:
getaddrinfo() looks up a node name and/or service name and returns a linked list of socket addresses and the information needed to use them. Optional hints let an application limit results by address family, socket type, protocol, or flags. freeaddrinfo() releases the returned list, and both functions must be thread-safe.

getnameinfo() converts a socket address into a node name and/or service name. The inet_pton() and inet_ntop() functions convert IPv4 or IPv6 addresses between numeric binary form and text. Address-testing macros identify special IPv6 address types and multicast scopes. The memo's security section says companion work on exposing IPv6 security mechanisms through the socket interface was being written.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs can ask one function for usable addresses from a host and service name, or turn an address back into names. Other functions convert addresses between text and binary forms.

items.title: Limit changes
items.text: Make conversion from IPv4 applications simpler.

items.title: Interoperate
items.text: Allow use with IPv4 and IPv6 hosts.

items.title: Align addresses
items.text: Place IPv6 address data on a 64-bit boundary.
